As far back as 2009, the government knew the lead was deteriorating and might blow up on its own. But it procrastinated. title: Trump is destroying the rule of law in the US – to protect himself and the tech titans he worships as new gods | Jonathan Freedland
author: Jonathan Freedland
categories: Donald Trump | US news | US foreign policy | Jensen Huang | Nvidia | Technology | AI (artificial intelligence) | Trump administration | US justice system | US politics | World news
description: To get Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, the president trampled on the justice system, national security and the trust America needs to do business in the global economy Don’t let the sex distract you. Or the lies or the boardroom intrigue or even the AI-generated bra, all of which could have come from an especially wild episode of Succession. Don’t let that lure you into thinking that the Jensen Huang affair is, as Donald Trump would have it, little more than a sex scandal involving a corporate maestro. It is much more serious than that. The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law. It can be hard to see that through the thicket of questions that surround this episode, each one of which, don’t get me wrong, merits attention. Consider the personal profit Trump made thanks to his re-installation of Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, the world’s leading maker of advanced AI chips. Breaking the norm observed by previous presidents who, keen to avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, either divested themselves of stock holdings or placed them in a blind trust, Trump cheerfully buys and sells stocks in companies whose fates he can influence. He saw the value of his shares in Nvidia plunge when Huang was forced out, following revelations that the CEO had had an affair with Alice Huang, reportedly an asset of Chinese intelligence. Last weekend Trump urged the board to reconsider; Huang was reinstated on Monday and Nvidia’s value promptly soared – putting $15m in Trump’s pocket . Not for the first time, he had used the power of his office to enrich himself. Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Gerald Grace obituary
author: Helena Grace
categories: Durham University | Teaching | Catholicism | Education | Education degree courses
description: My father, Gerald Grace, who has died aged 90, began his career as a history teacher, before becoming a lecturer and then eventually professor of education at Durham University. He devoted his later years to developing Catholic education into a recognised international field of study. In 1997, despite having retired the year before, he set up the Centre for Research and Development in Catholic Education (CRDCE) with the support of Peter Mortimore , director of the London Institute of Education (IOE). This was the first of its kind in Europe and established a survey of Catholic educational research across 30 countries. It spawned two publications: the International Handbook of Catholic Education (2007) and the journal International Studies in Catholic Education (2009), the first studies of research and scholarship in Catholic education. He was also a prolific author of books about education, including Faith, Mission and Challenge in Catholic Education (2016).

title: Alan Thornett obituary
author: Tony Richardson
categories: Trade unions | Industrial action | Automotive industry
description: In the postwar years, at a time when industry needed labour, British workers organised strongly in unions, and were able to raise their earnings. Among the most successful of them were the car workers. My friend Alan Thornett, who has died aged 89, was a trade unionist at the Morris Motors plant in Cowley, Oxford, and a key motor industry militant from the 1960s until the 80s. Alan was born in Abingdon, the son of Florence (nee Padgett), a glove maker, and Cyril, who worked on the railways. He left school at 15 to work on a farm, then spent three years in the army before starting in the Morris Motors assembly plant in 1959. He joined the Transport and General Workers’ Union (now Unite) and became a shop steward in 1964. In 1968 one-third of the registered strikes in Britain were in the Cowley assembly plant, many over piecework rates. By then Alan had become a deputy senior steward.

title: They crossed the doom loop of Groundhog Day with Nightmare on Elm Street. Voilà – it’s Peter Mandelson | Robert Hutton
author: Robert Hutton
categories: Peter Mandelson | Politics | Jensen Huang | UK news
description: He’s perennially disgraced and yet he just won’t go away – now he’s joined the latest Brexit debate. Isn’t there a mute button, or an exile plan that really works? What a week it has been for Indispensable Men. In the old days, if someone were forced to resign, whether as ambassador to Washington or boss of a trillion-dollar company, they would become what we quaintly used to call “disgraced”. Perhaps they would spend the rest of their days volunteering with a charity. Certainly, for a good decade afterwards, they would acquire the journalistic epithet “shamed” on first mention. Later – much later – they might be allowed back into public life, in some lesser role where they could be discreetly supervised, to check exactly how many emails they were sending to which people arranging what holidays. But what’s this we find over on news website UnHerd? Why, it’s a 2,000-word essay from one Peter Mandelson on the difficulties of rejoining the European Union. Mandelson … Mandelson. That name definitely rings a bell. Let’s see if there’s a clue at the bottom of the piece. Ah, yes: “Peter Mandelson is a former cabinet minister and EU Trade Commissioner.” That’s the chap: Gordon Brown’s former business secretary. Though I feel as if I’ve seen his name in the news a bit more recently than 2010. Might he be a “former” anything else?

title: Never mind EU student fees – it’s time to rethink the entire UK higher education system | Simon Jenkins
author: Simon Jenkins
categories: Universities | Higher education | Tuition fees | European Union | UK news | Higher education policy | Labour | Students
description: The last shake-up, in the 1960s, was based on pure anti-technological snobbery. Let’s put vocational learning back in the heart of our cities What is it about the EU student fees debate that means it has almost derailed Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset? Can the issue be that important? The answer is simple – and, I am sure, personal. Before Brexit, the EU’s citizens, among them its diplomats, were paying the same as UK citizens to have their children’s English perfected at a UK university. Now, some pay up to three times that figure . To put it mildly, they have an interest in persuading the UK government to slash fees. As of now, the issue is still deadlocked. The total cost of meeting the EU’s demand and reducing EU student fees to the new British rate of £9,790 a year has been put at an astronomical £570m a year for Russell group universities alone. Burnham has declined to answer the question of who would foot the bill. Indeed, it is difficult to understand why British taxpayers should subsidise the education of wealthy Europeans. But the cost would then fall on individual universities. The University of St Andrews estimates it would lose a devastating £12m annually. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

author: Andy Beckett
categories: Andy Burnham | Politics | Labour | Kemi Badenoch | UK news | Media
description: ‘Andy time’ may frustrate the media and voters impatient for change – but after years of short premierships and rushed policies, isn’t this the reset Westminster needs? Andy Burnham is making a lot of people impatient. Political journalists, pro-EU activists, climate campaigners, fossil-fuel lobbyists, recipients of welfare benefits, advocates of welfare cuts, enemies of neoliberalism, enthusiasts for renationalisation, members of the armed forces and even cabinet colleagues: all are waiting for the prime minister to make big decisions, and thus reveal the true nature of his administration, four months after its beginning. Since his Manchester mayoralty, some of Burnham’s co-workers have had a phrase for his tendency to take things at his own tempo: “Andy time”. He lets interesting conversations overrun, likes to ponder issues without being rushed, and pushes back crucial announcements. The unveiling of his 10-year plan – a typically ambitious but loose Burnham timespan, and one of his government’s pivotal moments – has been repeatedly delayed. According to the website Politico, it has been pencilled in for 17 December, the final day of the parliamentary calendar. Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

It is widely agreed that the choice of its next secretary general is critical – perhaps even existential. Unfortunately, that’s where agreement ends. Under the opaque selection system, security council members are privately polled on their views of each candidate. The proposed rule changes would add two new parts to the regulations that govern the census: One change would remove a question about race and ethnicity, while another would add a citizenship question. Also among the proposed changes is a line that would formally bar questions about sexual orientation from being included. The US census is critical in understanding the American population. Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal? The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. author: Editorial
categories: Wales | Andy Burnham | Labour | Cardiff | Rhun ap Iorwerth | Politics | UK news
description: The PM has summarily dismissed Welsh demands for further powers similar to those enjoyed in Scotland. The approach seems at odds with his consensual style As he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations. In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. In the case of policing, Mr Burnham is in the curious position of denying to Mr ap Iorwerth the type of power that he enjoyed as the mayor of Greater Manchester. He can barely hide his misogyny for Sarah Pochin, having written her off as a pisshead. Nor does he have a much higher opinion of Richard Tice, Zia Yusuf and the others. description: Defend those being targeted, even when the threat has not reached your door Welcome back to How We Win , a Guardian opinion series with bold ideas for America’s political future. In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. description: On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union. Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. I wholeheartedly agree with Andy Burnham when he said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe.” For years, the evidence has pointed in the same direction, that the UK economy is worse off as a result of Brexit. Trade barriers have increased, growth has suffered and businesses have been forced to navigate unnecessary bureaucracy. Many of the industries that Brexit supporters claimed would flourish have instead struggled. Fishing, farming, construction and touring musicians have all faced new obstacles, costs and restrictions. Meanwhile, younger generations have seen opportunities to study, work, travel and collaborate across Europe reduced through no fault of their own. description: In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday. That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election.
